title: Another List

jokes.text: Hank warms up the studio audience by reading the 'applause' cue card and then pretending he was kidding before asking someone to flick it — meta-theater about how manufactured audience response is.
jokes.setup: Hank reads aloud the instruction on a cue card that says 'applause' — breaking the fourth wall of late-night artifice.
jokes.punchline: He starts with 'No, I'm kidding' as if the audience caught him doing something embarrassing, then has the card flicked anyway — the gag is that the artifice is exposed and then immediately restored.
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders meta-move: exposing the machinery of late-night while also showing Hank's hapless earnestness. The joke works because Hank clearly doesn't see anything wrong with the cue card system, which makes his embarrassed 'no I'm kidding' more absurd. Good character integration.

dialogue.line: and now, because Larry's home catching up on his sex, Jon Stewart.

jokes.text: Hank's announcer intro: 'and now, because Larry's home catching up on his sex, Jon Stewart.'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night announcer intro framing explaining why a guest host is filling in.
jokes.punchline: 'Catching up on his sex' — a hilariously specific and inappropriate reason delivered in the formal announcer register, implying Larry's sex life is so behind schedule it requires dedicated catch-up sessions.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — maximum funny per word. The contrast between the formal announcer register and the phrase 'catching up on his sex' is the entire joke, and it's perfectly timed. 'Catching up on his sex' suggests Larry's sex life is a backlog, like email, which is both sad and absurd. Very quotable, very Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: So I was thinking, 'hey, Why not just save the money And go out with tori spelling?'

jokes.text: Jon Stewart pitching the Real Doll to Hank: 'Hank, actually, you might want to get good trade-in value on your old doll, actually, for these.'
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart is doing a bit about the new Real Doll sex toy on the air.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to suggest Hank already owns a sex doll and should trade it in — implying Hank is so lonely and pathetic that this is obvious.
jokes.explanation: Solid late-night joke that works because it targets Hank's well-established sad-sack persona. The 'actually' repeated twice is a nice Stewart verbal tic. Functions as both a bit and a character jab at Hank. Mid-tier for this show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I just feel like A wet burlap bag Full of monkey shit.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart's Tori Spelling punchline: 'So I was thinking, hey, why not just save the money and go out with Tori Spelling?'
jokes.setup: Real Dolls cost $5,000. They have fake breasts, synthetic hair, and are 'built for sex.'
jokes.punchline: Why spend $5,000 when Tori Spelling is the real-world equivalent and is available to date — implying she's fake and sexual-object-like.
jokes.explanation: A functional late-90s celebrity-roast-style joke. The structure is clean but it's a cheap shot at Tori Spelling's appearance/reputation rather than something genuinely clever. Works in the room, ages poorly. Mid-tier standup material.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that came across.

jokes.text: Larry asks about Jon Stewart's ratings. Staffer says a guest host always gets better ratings because 'no one has time to get sick of him.' Larry: 'So what are you saying? They're sick of the regular host?'
jokes.setup: Larry fishing for reassurance about Jon Stewart's ratings, clearly anxious.
jokes.punchline: Larry correctly interprets the diplomatic non-answer as an indictment of himself, which is both accurate and completely ignored by the staffer who denies it.
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders — his paranoid self-absorption leads him to correctly identify the subtext everyone is dancing around. The exchange is tight, economical, and deeply character-specific. His insecurity IS the punchline, and it's both funny and sad. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: You know, that's How you get the flu. You could wear Rubber gloves.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's true, And then I could, uh, Check their prostates, too.

jokes.text: Hank: 'When I'm sitting next to Jon Stewart, I just feel like a wet burlap bag full of monkey shit.'
jokes.setup: Hank is expressing relief that Larry is back, contrasting how he feels next to Larry vs. next to Jon Stewart.
jokes.punchline: The simile 'wet burlap bag full of monkey shit' — grotesquely specific and delivered with complete sincerity, expressing Hank's total collapse of self-esteem next to a younger, funnier man.
jokes.explanation: The standout line of the episode. 'Wet burlap bag full of monkey shit' is grotesquely specific, perfectly calibrated to Hank's verbose self-pity, and lands with total sincerity — he genuinely means it. The specificity (wet, burlap, full of, monkey shit) does tremendous work. This is a Hank line and only a Hank line. Deeply character-integrated, highly quotable, and structurally perfect as the punctuation to his comparison. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor — a different register but equal craft.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: We'd get more Of er's audience.

jokes.text: Larry's flat response to Hank's 'wet burlap bag' speech: 'Well, that came across.'
jokes.setup: Hank has delivered an unhinged, self-pitying monologue comparing himself to a bag of monkey shit.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response is a two-word deadpan that simultaneously dismisses Hank's emotional vulnerability and validates it — 'that came across' means 'yes, you are pathetic and it showed.'
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in economy. Four words that are simultaneously cruel, accurate, and funny. Larry's emotional negligence toward Hank is the engine of their dynamic, and this line is the perfect expression of it. The understatement IS the statement. Would score higher on impact but it's the setup-punchline pairing with joke #6 that really elevates both.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Why are you fucking With me like this? 'Hey now' is My catch phrase. I own it.

jokes.text: Hank tries to get a word in; Artie cuts him off so Larry can speak; Larry immediately parrots back exactly what Artie said he wanted to do.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Hank to let Larry speak for himself, suggesting Larry has something important to say.
jokes.punchline: Larry literally repeats Artie's words verbatim — 'I've got more important matters to address myself to' — proving he's just Artie's mouthpiece.
jokes.explanation: Efficient character comedy — Larry's dependence on Artie is shown, not told. The payoff is that Hank needed to hear it from Larry directly, and what he hears is Artie's words in Larry's mouth. The joke is about the show's power dynamics without a word wasted.

jokes.text: Network exec tells Larry he's losing to Keenan. Larry's suggested fix: run through the audience and shake hands like Leno. Larry: 'You know, that's how you get the flu.'
jokes.setup: Network exec suggests a more enthusiastic Leno-style entrance where Larry shakes everyone's hands.
jokes.punchline: Larry's objection is that shaking hands spreads the flu — a hypochondriac, germophobic non-sequitur that reveals his priorities.
jokes.explanation: Nicely character-specific — Larry's resistance to the network note is expressed through hypochondriac deflection rather than artistic objection, which is more revealing and funnier. Sets up the rubber glove escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: And, like the limited Mcrib sandwich-- Scrumptious, hot, And hard to get.

jokes.text: Network exec suggests rubber gloves for the handshaking entrance. Larry: 'That's true, and then I could, uh, check their prostates, too.'
jokes.setup: Exec suggests rubber gloves as a solution to the flu objection.
jokes.punchline: Larry escalates to prostate exams — if you're wearing rubber gloves and touching audience members, why not go all the way? Absurdist but logical.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation off the rubber gloves premise. The absurdist leap to prostate exams is unexpected but follows a perverse logic. The exec's 'we'd get more of ER's audience' callback makes it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Larry, she's never Done a nude scene.

jokes.text: Network exec responds to the prostate joke: 'We'd get more of ER's audience.' Larry: 'Okay, that's funny stuff.'
jokes.setup: Larry has made a prostate exam joke. The exec unexpectedly riffs back.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'okay, that's funny stuff' is condescending praise — a host acknowledging a civilian made a joke. The joke is Larry being surprised a network suit can be funny.
jokes.explanation: A modest but functional beat. Larry's slightly condescending acknowledgment of the exec's wit is character-consistent. Not a big laugh but adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is he retarded?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: No. He works In a shoe store. He looks just like you.

jokes.text: Network exec pulls out a photo to illustrate a different hairstyle. It turns out to be supermodel Christy Turlington. Larry, Artie, and the entire meeting devolves into everyone ogling her photo and asking if she's single.
jokes.setup: The exec is trying to make a serious point about Larry's hairstyle using a research photo.
jokes.punchline: The photo is Christy Turlington. All business stops. Larry and Artie immediately ask if she's married and who she's dating — the meeting collapses into hormone-driven distraction.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed scene derailment. The comedy is in the complete abandonment of the professional context — the hairstyle discussion evaporates the moment an attractive woman appears. Works as character comedy (Larry's shallowness) and as situational misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Fisher
dialogue.line: This is like A wet dream come true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, that's why We have the tarp.

jokes.text: Larry, mid-meeting about his show's survival, immediately pivots to: 'Is she married?' upon seeing Christy Turlington's photo.
jokes.setup: The network is trying to have a serious conversation about Larry's declining ratings.
jokes.punchline: Larry's first response to seeing a beautiful woman mid-crisis meeting is to ask about her availability — his libido completely overriding his professional anxiety.
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders characterization — the man's insecurities and libido are perfectly calibrated to be equally powerful and equally sabotaging. In a meeting about whether he'll lose his job, his first words are about a woman's relationship status. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What's it called? What-- uh... This song? Yeah. It's called, uh, this is track 3.

jokes.text: Larry asks about 'Skusi Baskin' — the exec corrects him: 'Suzie.' Larry asks: 'Suzie or Skusi?' Exec: 'Skusi.' Larry: 'Single?'
jokes.setup: Another photo appears in the meeting materials — clearly another attractive woman.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately asks 'Single?' — he cannot even process another attractive woman's name before pivoting to whether she's available. His priorities are completely transparent.
jokes.explanation: Running gag continuation — Larry derailing the business meeting with his romantic availability radar. The name confusion ('Skusi?') adds a small comic grace note. Economy is excellent — 'Single?' as a one-word punchline is very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Winona Ryder
dialogue.line: I'm not funny Or interesting, So I hope that's not Going to be a problem.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that Hasn't stopped Hank.

jokes.text: Beverly tells Larry the 'Hey Now' license plates he wanted are taken. The alternatives offered include: 'Hey Not, Haystack, Hey Mama, Hair Now.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been trying to get personalized license plates that say 'Hey Now' — Hank's catchphrase, apparently also coveted by Larry.
jokes.punchline: The alternate suggestions are deliberately terrible near-misses — 'Hey Not,' 'Haystack,' 'Hey Mama,' 'Hair Now' — an absurdist list that gets funnier with each iteration.
jokes.explanation: The list of near-miss license plate alternatives is the joke — 'Hair Now' is the best because it's both phonetically close and accidentally self-referential (see: the network's hairstyle note). 'Haystack' is delightfully random. Good absurdist comedy of the list format.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: I think last night One of the actors From melrose place Threw up on my door.

dialogue.speaker: Roger
dialogue.line: Ah, you're so fucking great. I love it.

jokes.text: Larry's reaction to the license plate alternatives: 'Why are you fucking with me like this? Hey Now is my catch phrase. I own it. I made it up.'
jokes.setup: Larry is furious that someone else has the 'Hey Now' license plates.
jokes.punchline: Larry claims ownership of 'Hey Now' as his catchphrase — but 'Hey Now' is actually Hank's catchphrase. Larry's self-aggrandizing claim to something that belongs to his sidekick is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Larry's belief that 'Hey Now' belongs to him — when it's definitively Hank's line — is a deeply revealing moment of ego. It also sets up the entire 'Hey Now' plate subplot with Paul Fisher. Larry's possessiveness over something that isn't his is very true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's funny. I thought I was the 'hey now' guy. Ha ha ha ha ha.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Fisher
dialogue.line: Not in valencia, my friend.

jokes.text: Artie asks who the person with the 'Hey Now' plates is. He's described as 'a big fan.' Artie: 'So?' Larry: 'All right. You're right. Bring him down to the set and I'll schmooze him, and he'll probably just give you the plates.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants the 'Hey Now' plates back from a fan who legally has them.
jokes.punchline: Larry's plan — schmooze the fan with star power and he'll voluntarily surrender his property — is delivered with complete confidence, as if this is a perfectly reasonable business strategy.
jokes.explanation: Character comedy rooted in Larry's celebrity narcissism — he genuinely believes his fame is so powerful that a fan will surrender their property out of star-struck gratitude. This is funny and also slightly pathetic.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You don't have to run. What if you just walk Through the audience? You walk. It doesn't Have to look like A fucking telethon.

jokes.text: Artie's plan: bring the plate-holder fan to the set so Larry can schmooze him; the implication is that Larry's star power will make a stranger voluntarily surrender property.
jokes.setup: Someone has the 'Hey Now' plates and Hank can't get them.
jokes.punchline: Artie's solution — parade Larry in front of the fan so he becomes 'star-struck' and just hands over his license plates — reveals the show's worldview: celebrity as a currency that bypasses all rational exchange.
jokes.explanation: Solid satirical beat about how celebrity operates in Hollywood. The assumption that a fan would just give up his plates is absurd but also kind of true to how these ecosystems work. Sets up the payoff scene.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's like A shooting gallery.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, i'll just run home And bring back My 7 mil. Remington mag.

jokes.text: Network exec says their research shows 18-34s want a 'snappier' theme song. Larry: 'How many of that demographic actually used the word snappy? 47%.'
jokes.setup: The network exec is citing research showing younger viewers want a snappier theme.
jokes.punchline: Larry mocks the research by questioning whether 47% of 18-34 year olds actually used the word 'snappy' — exposing the absurdity of translating focus group data into creative directives. Then the exec says '47%' without irony, making it worse.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry satire. The joke works on two levels: Larry's withering skepticism of research-speak AND the exec's earnest 47% answer, which confirms the absurdity. The immediate factual response to a rhetorical question is a perfect comic beat. Very Larry Sanders — this is exactly the kind of entertainment-industry-insider skewering the show does best.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He has colon cancer. I've got-- He's dying.

jokes.text: The proposed new theme song — a funky instrumental spec from the 'Singled Out' composer — plays in full, and Larry simply walks out of the room without a word.
jokes.setup: The network execs have commissioned a new theme song spec and are playing it for Larry with evident pride.
jokes.punchline: Larry's only response is to leave the room. No argument, no explanation. The walkout IS the review.
jokes.explanation: A great visual/behavioral comedy moment. The joke is entirely structural — the funky theme plays for 20+ seconds, building anticipation for a reaction, and Larry's response is silent departure. The staffer's confused 'He just walked out on us' confirms it. Maximum economy (zero words from Larry). Deeply character-specific — Larry would rather exit than dignify the question with a response. Excellent craft for a non-verbal beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're all fucking crazy.

jokes.text: After Larry walks out, staffer says: 'He just walked out on us.' Artie: 'No, he didn't.'
jokes.setup: Larry has demonstrably just walked out of the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat denial of the obvious — 'No, he didn't' — is the protective Artie move: cover for Larry at all costs, even when it's farcically transparent.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Artie beat. His job is to manage the relationship between Larry and the network, and he does it by denying reality with complete composure. Two words, maximum character definition. The economy and character integration are both exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I am nothing like that-- That sick fuck. He is a pathetic, Annoying nobody, And I am-- I am Hank fucking Kingsley.

jokes.text: Network exec reveals to Artie that Jon Stewart's numbers 'are the same, if not better, than Larry's. And he's a hell of a lot cheaper.'
jokes.setup: The execs have been dancing around the real purpose of their visit.
jokes.punchline: The blunt delivery of Jon Stewart's cost advantage — 'a hell of a lot cheaper' — as the actual bottom line after all the notes about hairstyles and theme songs is darkly funny. All the 'feedback' was window dressing.
jokes.explanation: Industry satire: the real reason for all the notes is money, not quality. The joke lands because it retrospectively reframes the entire meeting. Darkly funny in context of the show's final season meta-narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. Did I forget To say now?

jokes.text: Beverly tells Larry: 'Winona Ryder's never done a nude scene.' Larry laughs uproariously.
jokes.setup: Larry has asked Beverly to pull Winona Ryder's movies for pre-interview research.
jokes.punchline: Beverly preemptively addresses what she knows Larry actually wants to know — whether there are nude scenes — which he didn't ask but was obviously wondering. His loud laugh is the confession.
jokes.explanation: Great character-comedy efficiency. Beverly knows Larry so well she answers the question he didn't ask. The implicit joke is that 'research' means something very specific to Larry. His laughter is a perfect reaction beat — caught out and finding it funny himself. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Winona Ryder
dialogue.line: Everything's fine, Except I don't want To talk about the aliens Under water stuff. I'm so sick Of talking about that.

jokes.text: Larry points to a woman in what turns out to be a Visine ad and asks if they can book her on the show.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to give the network executives something — 'throw them a bone' — by booking an attractive guest.
jokes.punchline: The woman he's pointing to is in a Visine eye drop advertisement — not a celebrity, not even a person with a notable eye problem story. His 'research' into bookable talent is just pointing at attractive women.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag with a strong misdirect payoff. The reveal that it's a Visine ad is funny, then Larry's follow-up pitch — 'I can ask her how she got that thing in her eye' — is even funnier, showing he'd try to build an interview around absolutely nothing if the woman was attractive enough.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And you can go around, And you can say, 'Hey now' till Your dick falls off. But you know what, paul? That does not make you me!

jokes.text: Larry's pitch for the Visine woman: 'I can ask her how she got that thing in her eye. Maybe it's, uh—' Beverly: 'And she can wear whatever she wants.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to justify booking a woman from a Visine ad.
jokes.punchline: His interview pitch trails off ('maybe it's, uh—') because there IS no story, revealing the whole idea is pure attraction. Beverly's 'she can wear whatever she wants' is a knowing punctuation — she understands exactly what's happening.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of joke #24. The trailing '...uh—' doing real comedic work — the pause admits there's no pitch. Beverly finishing the thought exposes the charade. Works well as a tag.

dialogue.speaker: Paul Fisher
dialogue.line: I mean, with The show ending. What? You haven't heard?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Jon Stewart is Taking over for Larry.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Throw them a bone. But fake throw it and see if their heads move.'
jokes.setup: Larry says they need to 'throw the network guys a bone' by making some concessions.
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice is to fake-throw the bone like you're fooling a dog — revealing his contempt for the network executives, who he views as animals that can be misdirected.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Fake throw it and see if their heads move' is a perfect Artie line — contemptuous, strategic, funny, and built on a vivid dog metaphor. It's deeply character-integrated (Artie is the show's veteran fixer, seen it all, respects no one except Larry) and highly quotable. The economy is excellent — the image does all the work in one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: But didn't inhale.

jokes.text: Larry claims to be a big Smash Mouth fan, then can't name a single song when pressed.
jokes.setup: Larry says enthusiastically 'I'm a big fan of Smash Mouth, you know.' Someone asks what his favorite song is.
jokes.punchline: 'They're all — they're all good. Excuse me.' He deflects and leaves — he has no idea who Smash Mouth is.
jokes.explanation: Classic late-night host insincerity exposed. Larry's glib 'big fan' claim collapses instantly when challenged to name a song. The hasty exit is the confession. Good character comedy, relatable observation about show business insincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: Um, would you want to go out And get a bite to eat later? You know, maybe You want to pussy hunt?

jokes.text: Artie compares Larry's ratings crisis response to Dick Cavett, who 'compensated by screwing everything in the tristate area. With me, it's food.'
jokes.setup: Artie is observing that people under professional stress find compensatory behaviors.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'Cavett screwed everything in the tristate area' to 'with me, it's food' is a darkly funny self-assessment — Artie admits he's a stress eater while simultaneously making a great Cavett joke.
jokes.explanation: Artie at his best — self-deprecating, show-biz savvy, and darkly funny. The Cavett reference grounds it in real Hollywood lore. The pivot to 'with me, it's food' is perfectly delivered self-revelation. Highly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And now, because The charges were dropped, Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Hank launches into 'Little Bo Hank' riff: 'I'm little bo Hank, and I've lost my sheep in a—in a—in a poker game.'
jokes.setup: The conversation has turned to people finding compensation behaviors under stress.
jokes.punchline: Hank derails with a bizarre nursery rhyme riff in which Little Bo Peep's sheep are lost in a poker game — a complete non-sequitur that Hank seems genuinely pleased with.
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-amused non-sequitur riffing is a recurring character trait. The nursery rhyme adaptation is mildly absurd but doesn't fully land. The comedy is more in the context — Hank derailing a serious conversation — than in the joke itself.

jokes.text: Paul Fisher (the 'Hey Now' plate owner) arrives. Artie: 'He looks just like you.' [to Hank]. Larry: 'Is he retarded?' Artie: 'No, he works in a shoe store.'
jokes.setup: Paul Fisher arrives — a fan who has the 'Hey Now' license plates. He apparently physically resembles Hank.
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate question 'Is he retarded?' when told the man looks like Hank — implying Hank looks mentally disabled. Then Artie's 'No, he works in a shoe store' as if that's a meaningful distinction.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Larry's cruel implication about Hank's appearance, followed by Artie's non-answer ('shoe store') that neither confirms nor denies anything. The cruelty is softened by the absurdism of the shoe store distinction. The 'retarded' usage is dated and somewhat blunt — lowers the earned_vs_cheap score.

jokes.text: Paul Fisher snaps back at Hank: 'Could you crawl under here and blow me?' Hank: 'I don't do fat chicks.'
jokes.setup: Paul Fisher is apparently a Hank doppelgänger, and Hank is sizing him up condescendingly.
jokes.punchline: Paul's aggressive non-sequitur, followed by Hank's completely irrelevant response about 'fat chicks' — Hank either didn't hear the insult correctly or is deflecting with his own aggression.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the cross-wired aggression — two people insulting each other in completely incompatible registers. Hank's non-answer about 'fat chicks' to a male aggressor is absurd. Somewhat crude but functional in context.

jokes.text: Paul Fisher gets to sit in Hank's chair and says: 'Live on tape from Hollywood, it's me.' Then: 'This is like a wet dream come true.' Hank: 'Well, that's why we have the tarp.'
jokes.setup: Paul is seated at the announce desk, living out a fantasy, and says it's 'like a wet dream come true.'
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate 'Well, that's why we have the tarp' — deadpan, as if this is standard operating procedure, implying the announcer's desk has needed protective covering before.
jokes.explanation: A great tight joke. 'That's why we have the tarp' lands perfectly because it's delivered as pure matter-of-fact facility management, as if Hank has had to deal with this before. The economy is excellent, the setup/payoff structure is crisp, and the image is both absurd and vivid. Hank's deadpan delivery sells it as a real protocol.

jokes.text: Hank's response to Paul's 'wet dream' excitement about sitting in the chair: 'Well, that's why we have the tarp.'
jokes.setup: Paul exclaims 'This is like a wet dream come true!' about sitting in Hank's chair.
jokes.punchline: Hank: 'Well, that's why we have the tarp.' — delivered completely straight, as if the chair has a tarp for exactly this eventuality.
jokes.explanation: A textbook perfect economy joke. The setup is handed to Hank by Paul's clichéd exclamation; Hank's response takes the idiom literally with one word ('tarp') that creates an immediate, vivid, disgusting image. The deadpan delivery implied by the script makes it even better. This is what an 8 looks like: genuinely surprising, impeccably constructed, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Larry greets Smash Mouth after their performance. He tells the lead singer it's his 'favorite song.' Singer asks what it's called. Larry: 'This song? Yeah. It's called, uh... this is track 3.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just told Smash Mouth he's a 'great big fan' and their performance is his 'favorite song.'
jokes.punchline: He can't name the song. His best answer is 'track 3' — confirming he knows nothing about the band.
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the earlier Smash Mouth joke. 'Track 3' is the ideal specific-yet-useless answer — it proves he's been faking. The singer's brief laugh before the scene moves on acknowledges the awkwardness without overdoing it. Strong running gag payoff.

jokes.text: Larry to Winona Ryder: 'I'm not funny or interesting, so I hope that's not going to be a problem.' Winona: 'Well, that hasn't stopped Hank.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Winona are getting to know each other backstage. Larry jokes self-deprecatingly that he's not funny or interesting.
jokes.punchline: Winona Ryder claps back: 'Well, that hasn't stopped Hank' — a perfect, crisp, celebrity-delivered burn on Hank's unfunniness.
jokes.explanation: Excellent tight joke. The setup is mild self-deprecation; the punchline pivots to a more deserving target (Hank) with perfect economy. 'That hasn't stopped Hank' is five words that do enormous work. Works especially well because it comes from a celebrity who has no reason to have formed opinions about Hank — it means Hank's reputation for being unfunny precedes him.

jokes.text: Winona: 'It'll just kind of be like this. Yeah, except there's going to be millions of people watching.' Larry: 'Yeah, well, I'll tell them to turn their sets off before you come on.' Winona: 'A lot of them do that on their own, anyway.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to reassure Winona that the interview will be casual. She points out millions will be watching.
jokes.punchline: Larry jokes he'll tell them to turn off; Winona fires back that they already do — a self-deprecating joke that turns his dismissal into a ratings burn on Larry himself.
jokes.explanation: Two-joke exchange where the second joke (Winona's) lands harder. 'A lot of them do that on their own, anyway' is a clean, economical ratings self-burn — and it lands as a genuine zinger. Works as both a laugh line and a thematic callback to the episode's central crisis (Larry's falling ratings).

jokes.text: Artie presents the updated set to the network execs: 'Voilà! No coffee table, the enhanced greenery.' Exec: 'That wasn't even one of our notes.' Artie: 'Well, we're way ahead of you, then.'
jokes.setup: Artie is showing off changes to the set, trying to placate the network.
jokes.punchline: The network exec says the greenery change 'wasn't even one of their notes' — meaning Artie changed something that wasn't requested. Artie spins this as being 'ahead' of them — the ultimate power move.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Artie — he's done the wrong thing and immediately reframes it as superiority. 'We're way ahead of you, then' takes an error and converts it into a power flex with zero pause for shame. Artie's contempt for network executives is the show's running engine and this is an excellent small expression of it.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart arrives backstage. Network execs: 'Oh, you're so fucking great. I love it.' Jon: 'I think one of the actors from Melrose Place threw up on my door last night.'
jokes.setup: Network exec greets Jon Stewart with exaggerated enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: Jon's response isn't a thanks but a casual anecdote about a Melrose Place actor vomiting on his hotel room door — a perfectly calibrated late-90s Hollywood-adjacent detail.
jokes.explanation: A good texture moment — it places Jon in the Chateau Marmont ecosystem (the rock and roll Hollywood world) while the vomiting detail is both specific and absurd. The exec's response ('You're so fucking great') as if this is a cool story rather than a problem is the real joke.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart complains to someone that Larry is avoiding him: 'Earlier when I crossed by in the hallway, he didn't say Hey Jon.' Then he doubles back to confirm it was him.
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart has become paranoid that Larry is avoiding him, despite this being the show's home turf.
jokes.punchline: His evidence — that Larry didn't say 'Hey Jon' as he crossed the hallway — and his careful re-crossing to confirm it was indeed Larry — is the behavior of a desperate, insecure person. The comedy is in the extreme vulnerability behind the elaborate surveillance operation.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-comedy. Jon Stewart — the guy who might replace Larry — is just as insecure and needy as Larry. The 'hallway crossing' surveillance is elaborately described with real comic timing. The comedy is in how much work he puts into assessing minimal social signals.

jokes.text: Hank offers Paul (the fan lookalike) his expensive suit, framing it as generosity, then reveals the real trade he wants: the 'Hey Now' license plates.
jokes.setup: Hank tells Paul he can keep the suit and acts magnanimous.
jokes.punchline: The suit is a Trojan horse — Hank wants Paul's license plates ('something that would go on my car'). His elaborate setup for what turns out to be a negotiation reveals Hank's transactional nature.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the license plate running gag. Hank's manipulation is transparent to everyone watching but he executes it with complete sincerity. Advances the plot while staying funny.

jokes.text: Paul Fisher insists: 'Hey, I'm the Hey Now guy.' Hank: 'That's funny. I thought I was the Hey Now guy.' Paul: 'Ha ha ha ha. Not in Valencia, my friend.'
jokes.setup: Paul has been given access to Hank's world and is now claiming territorial ownership of the catchphrase.
jokes.punchline: 'Not in Valencia, my friend' — Paul's claim that 'Hey Now' belongs to him in Valencia. The absurdity of geographically dividing a catchphrase, delivered with complete seriousness by a shoe store employee.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'Not in Valencia, my friend' is absurdly specific and completely committed — Paul genuinely believes he owns 'Hey Now' in the Valencia area, as if catchphrases have regional licensing. The economy is excellent, the specificity of 'Valencia' rather than a generic location is key, and it works as both a standalone joke and a perfect escalation of the catchphrase turf war.

jokes.text: Larry, spotting Jon Stewart approaching in the hallway: 'That's Jon Stewart. It's like a shooting gallery.' Artie: 'Well, I'll just run home and bring back my 7 mil. Remington mag.'
jokes.setup: Larry doesn't want to see Jon Stewart before the show and is watching him approach.
jokes.punchline: Artie's offer to get his Remington rifle — volunteering to shoot Jon Stewart — is delivered with the same casual helpfulness as offering to bring coffee.
jokes.explanation: Great Artie dark comedy. The specificity of '7 mil. Remington mag' — the caliber, the model — suggests Artie has actually thought about this, which is funnier than a generic 'I'll shoot him.' Artie's casual homicidal helpfulness is a recurring character note done very well here.

jokes.text: Artie's response to Jon Stewart's paranoia: 'He fucking loves you. We all do.'
jokes.setup: Jon is convinced Larry is avoiding him. Artie needs to manage his emotions.
jokes.punchline: Artie's reassurance — 'He fucking loves you. We all do.' — delivered with zero warmth but complete firmness, is funny precisely because it's the opposite of how you'd comfort someone.
jokes.explanation: Artie's way of delivering comfort is through terse, profane commands — 'He fucking loves you' sounds like a threat. The humor is in the complete absence of warmth in what is technically a warm statement. Perfect Artie.

jokes.text: Artie bribes Jon Stewart to stay calm before the show with 'sliced pineapple, tiger shrimp, and your favorite, a pack of Camel Lights.' Jon: 'That's good. That's good.'
jokes.setup: Artie is managing Jon Stewart's pre-show anxiety.
jokes.punchline: The combination of healthy snacks and cigarettes as equal items in a 'comfort package' — and that Camel Lights are specifically Jon's 'favorite' — is an absurdly specific character detail delivered without any comment.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the juxtaposition of healthy dressing room snacks with cigarettes as the crown jewel of the comfort package. Low-key funny, more texture than punchline.

jokes.text: Hank forces Beverly to reveal that Phil doesn't just imitate Artie — 'he captures you.' Artie: 'He captures me?' Beverly: 'Yeah. Captures you.'
jokes.setup: Artie has tried to retract the Phil imitation slip. Hank keeps pressing.
jokes.punchline: The upgrade from 'imitates' to 'captures' is devastating — it implies Phil's version of Artie is so accurate it's definitional. Artie's repeated 'He captures me?' is existential horror delivered as small talk.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation. The word 'captures' is the perfect upgrade — more devastating than 'imitates' or 'impersonates' because it implies total essence-capture. Artie's repeated 'He captures me?' is Rip Torn showing genuine wounded pride under the gruff exterior. The whole sequence mirrors the Hank/Paul Fisher subplot and deepens both. High rewatch value because you know where it's going.

jokes.text: Artie's explosion: 'You listen, you little fruit basket. I am nothing like that—that sick fuck. He is a pathetic, annoying nobody, and I am—I am Hank fucking Kingsley.'
jokes.setup: Wait — this is Hank, not Artie. Hank has been told Phil 'captures' him. He explodes.
jokes.punchline: Hank's volcanic rage and the climactic self-identification — 'I am Hank fucking Kingsley' — as the declaration of uniqueness, said with total sincerity and zero self-awareness. The 'fruit basket' insult is also absurdly quaint.
jokes.explanation: Jeffrey Tambor showcase moment. 'I am Hank fucking Kingsley' as the final declaration of identity after a meltdown about being replaceable — delivered with total sincerity — is both hilarious and oddly moving. The humor is in the gap between Hank's enormous self-regard and his actual status (a sidekick to a fading host). 'Fruit basket' as an insult is also perfectly Hank — old-fashioned, slightly impotent, yet committed. High quotability, high character integration.

jokes.text: Beverly's response to Hank's 'I am Hank fucking Kingsley' eruption: 'That's what I was saying.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just delivered a full screaming declaration of self.
jokes.punchline: Beverly calmly says 'that's what I was saying' — implying she was making the same point all along, just more quietly. She was saying he's Hank Kingsley; he screamed it at the ceiling.
jokes.explanation: The perfect punctuation to joke #44. Five words that completely deflate Hank's self-righteous explosion — she was agreeing with him the whole time. Perfect economy (maximum funny per word), excellent structure (timing off Hank's peak), and highly character-integrated (Beverly as the unflappable handler). One of the episode's best comedy beats.

jokes.text: Beverly leaves. Hank calls after her: 'I'm sorry. Did I forget to say now?' Pause. 'There you go.'
jokes.setup: Hank has exploded at Beverly about his identity. She leaves without acknowledging him.
jokes.punchline: Hank tries to end the encounter with his catchphrase — adding 'now' to his apology as if that's the issue — then congratulates himself: 'There you go.' He's recovered his brand identity through the catchphrase.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful coda to the whole sequence. After the existential crisis about his identity, Hank reasserts himself through the catchphrase — proving that 'Hey Now' IS Hank's identity. 'There you go' as self-congratulation after a disastrous conversation is both sad and funny. Deeply character-integrated.

jokes.text: Larry stumbles into Winona's dressing room, flustered: 'I'm sorry. I thought the door was— No. Come on in.' Then trails off with: 'Anything—everything under control you want to talk about and so forth?'
jokes.setup: Larry has walked in on Winona — probably mid-preparation — and is flustered.
jokes.punchline: 'Everything under control you want to talk about and so forth?' is grammatically collapsed sentence from a man trying to be smooth and failing completely. The trailing 'and so forth' is the tell — he has nothing.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-comedy from Garry Shandling. The sentence structure breakdown — 'anything—everything under control you want to talk about and so forth' — is very true to how people sound when they're nervous. Larry can hold a national audience but can't function around an attractive woman. Character-specific and relatable.

jokes.text: Winona tells Larry she doesn't want to talk about 'the aliens under water stuff.' Larry: 'Don't need to. Don't need to.' Then confidently says 'I'll see you out there. We'll... do that. Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Winona is setting interview boundaries — she doesn't want to discuss whatever 'aliens underwater' refers to.
jokes.punchline: Larry's eager 'Don't need to. Don't need to.' and then the completely empty sign-off 'We'll... do that. Thanks.' — he agrees to absolutely nothing and says it confidently.
jokes.explanation: 'We'll... do that. Thanks' is a great non-commitment — he has no idea what she just said but he's nodding along. The 'aliens under water' reference is also a funny throwaway that implies something absurd has happened in Winona's career/publicity cycle.

jokes.text: Larry warns Hank not to help Jon Stewart on stage because 'the network has gone sweet on Jon Stewart.' Hank immediately: 'Is Stewart taking over the show?'
jokes.setup: Artie has told Larry not to make things worse by helping Stewart. Larry tries to pass this on to Hank with some subtlety.
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately jumps to 'Is Stewart taking over?' — the maximum catastrophic interpretation of the minimum information. Artie: 'Oh, christ. You didn't hear anything. Understand?' Hank: 'What do you mean? I heard everything.'
jokes.explanation: Good Hank characterization. His immediate leap to worst-case scenario ('taking over the show') and his literal interpretation of Artie's 'you didn't hear anything' are both perfectly Hank. The exchange is tight and well-structured.

jokes.text: Hank, alone before going on: 'He's gonna step all over my punch lines now. I'm gonna go out there and he's gonna fuck me. It's so obvious.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just learned (incorrectly, sort of) that Jon Stewart might take over. He's about to go on air.
jokes.punchline: Hank's paranoid certainty that Stewart will sabotage his punch lines — as if Hank's punch lines are a valuable commodity worth stealing — is both delusional and pitiable.
jokes.explanation: More Hank self-pity/paranoia. The comedy is in his certainty that his punch lines are valuable enough to steal, and his use of 'fuck me' as the end result of being upstaged. Character consistent but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: On the air, Hank introduces Larry by begrudgingly giving Paul Fisher the license plates back: 'Listen, I'd rather give you my mother's arm, but a deal's a deal.'
jokes.setup: Hank has to hand over the plates to get the photo with Larry's arm around Paul.
jokes.punchline: 'I'd rather give you my mother's arm' — grotesquely specific, implying his mother's arm is more precious to him than anything else, and he'd sacrifice it rather than the plates. The absurdity of the comparison.
jokes.explanation: A great dark-comedy line. 'My mother's arm' is a perfectly grotesque and specific thing to offer instead of license plates — it reveals both Hank's attachment to the plates and his Hank-specific mode of hyperbole. Economical and character-saturated.

jokes.text: Paul refuses the plates back and tells Hank he can keep the suit AND the plates and 'say Hey Now till your dick falls off. But that does not make you me! Because I am—I'm deep. I'm complicated, and I cannot be defined by what you see on your television.'
jokes.setup: Hank has given Paul the plates and the suit. Paul doesn't want the plates now.
jokes.punchline: Wait — this is Hank speaking, retracting the plates, launching into his 'I am deep, I am complicated' speech — a direct echo of his earlier 'I am Hank fucking Kingsley' meltdown but in a new context. The repetition of the existential crisis is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A great callback to the episode's central Hank theme. 'I cannot be defined by what you see on your television' is both grandiose and heartbreaking — Hank ONLY exists on television. The joke is the gap between his self-image and reality. High character integration, excellent running gag architecture.

jokes.text: Paul Fisher reveals to Hank that 'Jon Stewart is taking over for Larry' — and his source is 'Artie.'
jokes.setup: Hank was trying to explain why the plates don't matter anymore now that 'the show is ending.'
jokes.punchline: Paul learned this from Artie — the very man who told everyone not to tell Larry. Artie has accidentally (or deliberately?) leaked the exact information he was trying to contain, to a random fan who then told Hank on live TV.
jokes.explanation: A plot-comedy payoff. The revelation that Artie — the show's supreme information controller — leaked the biggest secret to a random fan is a great ironic twist. The comedy is structural (farce logic where information travels to exactly the wrong person) and it has thematic weight (nothing can be controlled). Strong setup-to-payoff architecture.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart's on-air monologue: Monica Lewinsky 'apparently says she did perform oral sex, but didn't inhale.'
jokes.setup: Jon is doing Clinton/Lewinsky material — the dominant news story of 1998.
jokes.punchline: The 'didn't inhale' callback to Clinton's marijuana non-admission — applied to oral sex — is a wordplay pun that recontextualizes Clinton's famous dodge in a sexual setting.
jokes.explanation: A tight, economical political joke that works through the double-meaning of 'inhale.' The Clinton/marijuana callback is clever and the structure is clean. Standup material — not as character-integrated as the best sitcom moments, but genuinely well-constructed.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart: 'What I thought was interesting — my concern is what happens when the sex stops. I literally — I've gone 4 years without having any oral sex, and if I was near a nuclear button, I'd have pushed it.'
jokes.setup: Jon is segueing from Clinton's sex scandal to his own celibacy.
jokes.punchline: Four years without oral sex would make him push a nuclear button — the comic escalation from personal frustration to geopolitical catastrophe. The 'nuclear button' punchline is both absurd and darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The logic — sexual frustration leads to nuclear apocalypse — is absurdist but follows comedic logic. Dark subversive territory. Above-average standup material for late night.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart: 'I belong to a group called Sex Without Partners.' Larry: 'Oh, really?' Jon: 'How's that going?' Jon: 'Not bad. I'm the treasurer.'
jokes.setup: Jon is continuing the celibacy/sex deprivation thread.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm the treasurer' of Sex Without Partners — the joke is that this club has organizational structure, with officers, and Jon's role is treasurer. The institutional structure of a celibacy support group is the absurdist element.
jokes.explanation: Very tight absurdist joke. 'I'm the treasurer' is the perfect specific detail — not president, not member, treasurer — implying organizational dedication to one's own sexlessness. Economy is excellent. The standup penalty applies but this is genuinely good joke construction.

jokes.text: Jon Stewart riffs on his cat: 'It only takes cats about 30 seconds to have sex. But hours to catch one.'
jokes.setup: Jon has been discussing his neutered cat and animal sexuality.
jokes.punchline: 'Hours to catch one' — the 'one' is ambiguous: catching a cat for breeding or catching a sexual partner. The double meaning is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A clean double-meaning joke. 'Hours to catch one' working on two levels is efficient and structurally sound. Not particularly original but executed well.

jokes.text: Jon discusses a hairless cat on a cat show TV video: 'They're having trouble breeding him.' Larry: 'No kidding.' Jon: 'Who wants to have sex with a hairless cat?'
jokes.setup: Jon is describing a hairless cat seen on TV who 'they're having trouble breeding.'
jokes.punchline: 'Who wants to have sex with a hairless cat?' — the rhetorical question makes the answer (nobody) obvious while also being a slightly disturbing image.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational humor. The joke is obvious but delivered efficiently. Larry's 'No kidding' straight-man response works in the interview context. Below-average for this episode.

jokes.text: After the interview, Jon asks Larry: 'Would you want to go out and get a bite to eat later? You know, maybe you want to pussy hunt?'
jokes.setup: The on-air interview has ended warmly. Jon is making post-show social plans.
jokes.punchline: 'Pussy hunt' — Jon's blunt term for their mutual interest in pursuing women. The cringe is in the explicit nature of the phrase compared to the professional context, and in how it reveals that both men relate to women primarily as targets.
jokes.explanation: A cringe moment that works because it's said casually in a semi-professional context. Also bonds Larry and Jon as fundamentally similar — both are essentially the same guy with the same priorities. Somewhat crude but serves character work.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Larry about the show's crisis while Larry pretends he wasn't aware: 'The show is in trouble. Are you aware of that?' Larry: 'Yes, I am.' Artie: 'Well, were you planning on saying anything about it?' Larry: 'I believe I did, sir.' Artie: 'I don't recall.' Larry: 'Well, I'm sorry, sir. I thought beating you over the head with this would be sufficient.'
jokes.setup: The network crisis has been simmering all episode. Artie finally confronts Larry directly.
jokes.punchline: Larry and Artie's exchange parodies formal corporate language — 'I believe I did, sir' / 'I don't recall' / 'I thought beating you over the head with this would be sufficient' — Artie's version of saying 'I told you so' is delivered with mock deference that barely conceals fury.
jokes.explanation: 'I thought beating you over the head with this would be sufficient' is a great Artie line — expressing his frustration at Larry's emotional avoidance while also admitting it didn't work. The formal 'sir' register throughout makes the frustration funnier. Very character-integrated.

jokes.text: Artie's penultimate speech: 'Through all the years we've been together, I've always tried to protect you from the bullshit. But I can't anymore. You're gonna have to decide this for yourself, Sonny Boy.'
jokes.setup: The show is in genuine existential trouble. Artie is telling Larry he can't manage this one.
jokes.punchline: 'Sonny Boy' — the paternal diminutive after a serious speech — is the punctuation. It's funny because of how it reframes their relationship (Artie as exhausted father, Larry as overgrown child) and because the gravity of the speech is slightly punctured by the affectionate tag.
jokes.explanation: This moment walks the line between comedy and drama — it's the show working in its most characteristic register. The comedy is in 'Sonny Boy' and in the implication that Artie has ALWAYS protected Larry from the bullshit, which we believe completely. The scene is mostly dramatic but earns its place here.

jokes.text: Hank's final announcer intro: 'And now, because the charges were dropped, Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Episode-opening intro had Larry absent 'catching up on his sex.' Now for the real show Larry is back. The announcer intro needs a reason.
jokes.punchline: 'Because the charges were dropped' — implying Larry was briefly under criminal charges. No explanation, no specifics, delivered in full announcer voice with the same formality as 'catching up on his sex.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best single joke. 'Because the charges were dropped' is the perfect callback to the opening's 'catching up on his sex' — same structure, same delivery, maximum absurdist implication. It implies criminal charges without specifying what for, trusting the audience to laugh at the void where an explanation should be. The economy is near-perfect, the structure (as a bookend callback to the cold open) is elegant, and it's immediately quotable. This is what a great tag feels like — it reframes everything that came before and ends the episode on a high.

tmdb_overview: Larry's ratings are slipping and the suits are looking to replace him with regular guest host Jon Stewart. Hank tries to trade for a fan's ""Hey Now"" license plates.
